sections.text: Access, gender and quality education (SDG 4, 5 and 10): TSU educates 30,976 students from all 36 states and the FCT, including every one of Taraba State’s 16 local government areas. It offers 78 NUC-accredited programmes, with 24 more approved for 2026/2027, including B.Ed. Special Needs Education and B.Ed. Sustainable Development Studies. Women make up 43.6% of students and 44.7% of the 2025/2026 intake (4,161 of 9,303).

Health, water and well-being (SDG 3 and 6): the Faculty of Health Sciences has 6,338 students in Public Health, Environmental Health, Medical Laboratory Science and Nursing. Research covers nationwide mapping of malaria mosquito species (PLOS ONE, 2025), the safety of calabash chalk eaten by pregnant women, antimicrobial resistance and medicinal plants, and agro-chemical pollution of rivers around Jalingo.

Food, land and climate (SDG 2, 13 and 15): the Faculty of Agriculture teaches 1,193 students, and a B.Sc. Meteorology and Climate Studies starts in 2026/2027. Research covers soils, indigenous mushrooms and probiotic fermented foods; flood risk, land use change and soil erosion; and the plant biodiversity of Gashaka Gumti National Park, Nigeria’s largest national park.

sections.heading: Clean Energy and Infrastructure
sections.intro: SDG 7 and SDG 9: solar power keeps TSU’s key buildings running 24 hours a day, and generators are rarely needed in these buildings.

sections.text: Power, solar and internet coverage are set out building by building on the Power & ICT Reliability page.

Decent work, peace and partnerships (SDG 8, 16 and 17): 3,446 students in Management Sciences, the Entrepreneurship Directorate and a new B.Ed. Entrepreneurship; 887 students in Peace and Conflict Studies and 1,473 in Political Science and International Relations, with research on kidnapping and national security and press coverage of the #EndSARS protests; Dr Nsemba Edward Lenshie ranks 1st in Nigeria for peacebuilding and international security research (Scholarly Index, 2026); and co-authored research with 24 institutions in 18 countries.

summary: How TSU keeps its key academic and administrative facilities powered and connected: grid electricity, solar power, backup generators, 100 Mbps internet and Starlink satellite links.

sections.heading: Power Supply by Facility
sections.intro: Each key facility draws on more than one power source, so teaching, examinations, library services and administration continue when grid supply fails. Eight facilities combine grid, solar and generator supply; the TETFund ICT Experience Centre runs on grid and solar.

sections.heading: Solar Power Installations
sections.intro: All nine key facilities have solar systems. kVA is the inverter rating (how much load the system can carry at once); kWh is the battery storage (how long it can run). Capacities as reported by the university.

sections.heading: Buildings on the Grid
sections.intro: Every university building is connected to the national grid. Grid supply averages about 4 hours a day, so solar and generators provide the rest: generators are rarely needed in the key facilities with solar, and other faculty buildings use at least 2 hours of generator power a day.

title: Institutional AI Policy
summary: TSU’s draft policy on the responsible and ethical use of artificial intelligence, including generative AI, in teaching, assessment, research and administration, now before Senate for approval.

cells: Responsible and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Policy
All students, academic and non-teaching staff, researchers, visiting scholars, contractors and consultants, and all AI systems used for University purposes
Senate, with oversight by the Governing Council
At least every two years, or sooner if technology, law or regulation changes
AI supports human decisions but never replaces accountable human judgement on grades, admissions, discipline, employment or finance.
Each assessment is classed as A (AI prohibited), B (restricted), C (permitted) or D (required), and students are told in advance.
Students, staff and researchers declare material AI use, using the model declarations in the policy.
AI must not fabricate data, references or results, and cannot be listed as an author.
Personal data, student records, examination material and unpublished research must not be entered into unapproved AI tools.
An AI-detector score alone is never treated as proof of misconduct, and affected people can ask for human review.
Users check AI output for bias, and the University will work to reduce unequal access to paid AI tools.
Regular training for students and staff on verification, citation, privacy, bias, copyright and assessment design.
Approve and oversee the policy and major amendments
Set AI rules for each assessment and promote AI literacy
Secure AI infrastructure, risk assessment and technical guidance
Training in information literacy, citation and source checking
AI guidance in research integrity and supervision
